blocks.text: Give each dependency or consumer its own bounded share of resources, so one failure cannot consume everything.

The name comes from ship compartments: a breach floods one section, not the hull. Software bulkheads cap the **concurrency** each downstream or tenant may use, through separate thread pools, semaphores or connection pools. When one dependency stalls, only its compartment fills; the others keep working.

items: **Semaphore bulkhead:** counts concurrent calls on the caller's thread; cheap.
**Thread-pool bulkhead:** a dedicated pool and queue per dependency; isolates blocking calls.
**Reject fast** when full instead of queueing without bound.

blocks.text: The size of a compartment is a capacity decision: concurrency is roughly throughput times latency (Little's law).

cards.expectedOutput:

walkthrough.note: A dedicated, unchecked rejection tells callers the compartment is full, so they can degrade instead of waiting.
A `Semaphore` is the compartment. `tryAcquire` never blocks, and `finally` returns the permit even when the operation throws.
One bulkhead per dependency. Inventory slowness can consume at most two permits and never touches payments.
Two virtual threads hold both inventory permits. `entered.await()` guarantees both are inside, so the next outcome is deterministic.

blocks.text: A reporting service that shares a pool with checkout.

A web app uses one thread pool for everything. A new reporting endpoint runs slow queries, and during month-end all threads end up inside it. Checkout requests queue behind them and time out, though checkout itself is healthy. Giving reporting its own pool of ten and checkout its own of fifty means a reporting storm degrades reporting only.
Payoff: the blast radius of a slow dependency is its compartment, and the core business path stays available.

lists.title: Use when
items: One slow dependency could exhaust threads or connections shared with healthy ones.
Tenants or priorities must not starve each other.
Failure should degrade a feature, not the whole service.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Load is uniform and a single well-sized pool already serves it.
Splitting would leave each compartment too small to absorb normal bursts.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Compartments sized by guess; measure latency and concurrency first.
Without timeouts, permits are held forever and the compartment stays full.
Unbounded queues in a thread-pool bulkhead hide the saturation.
Idle compartments waste capacity that others could use.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Virtual threads make threads cheap, so a semaphore per dependency is the idiomatic bulkhead.
Thread-pool bulkheads still make sense to isolate CPU-bound or blocking native calls.

rows.difference: The bulkhead limits how many calls are in flight; the breaker stops calls based on past failures. The bulkhead protects you immediately, the breaker after evidence.
A rate limiter bounds arrivals per unit of time. A bulkhead bounds concurrent work in progress, regardless of how fast it arrived.
Timeouts release permits held by slow calls. Without them a bulkhead only slows the moment it fills.
A thread-pool bulkhead is a dedicated pool per dependency; the pattern is the partitioning, not the pool.

options.why: Each downstream gets its own bounded share of concurrency, and excess work is rejected rather than queued.
Permits are returned when work finishes, so this bounds concurrency, not the number of arrivals per second.
Rejection depends on how many calls are running now, not on a history of failures.

exercises.scenario: An API serves three tenants from one worker pool. Tenant A launched a batch that sends a thousand slow queries; tenants B and C now see timeouts although their own traffic is small and normal.
exercises.prompt: Which pattern addresses the root cause?

options.why: Per-tenant concurrency limits keep A's backlog from consuming the capacity B and C depend on.
B and C would retry into the same saturated pool and make it worse.
A's queries are slow and probably unique; caching does not stop them from occupying workers.
Nothing downstream is failing; the shared pool is being monopolized.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that undermines this bulkhead.
exercises.explanation: `acquire()` blocks when all permits are taken, so callers pile up behind a saturated dependency and the isolation is lost. Use `tryAcquire()` (or a short timeout) and reject.
Reserve a permit first and reject if none; the try block starts only after the permit is held, and finally guarantees its release.

exercises.prompt: Explain what a bulkhead isolates, how it differs from a rate limiter, and why it needs timeouts.

modelAnswer.text: A bulkhead gives each dependency or tenant its own cap on concurrent work, so one slow dependency can fill only its compartment. A rate limiter bounds arrivals per time; a bulkhead bounds work in flight. Permits are held while a call runs, so timeouts are required or a hung call keeps its permit forever.

keyPoints: Separate bounded compartments per dependency or tenant
Caps concurrency (work in flight), not arrival rate
Reject fast when full rather than queue unboundedly
